issues.subcategory: simulated data presented as real results
issues.description: The manuscript explicitly states in multiple places that the Method and Results sections were written using a randomized dataset produced by Qualtrics to simulate what the sections will look like after data collection. This means all reported statistics, means, standard deviations, F-values, p-values, effect sizes, and confidence intervals are fabricated from random data, not real participant responses. Publishing or submitting a manuscript with simulated results as if they were real findings is a fundamental reporting integrity problem. Readers cannot evaluate the actual findings because none exist yet.
issues.quote: [IMPORTANT: Method and results sections were written using randomized dataset produced by Qualtrics to simulate what these sections will look like after data collection. These will be updated following the data collection.]

issues.subcategory: abstract reports simulated results without clear disclosure
issues.description: The abstract reports specific findings (e.g., 'we generated a dummy set of samples in the Qualtrics survey (N = 1000) and found no empirical support for the effect of analytical reasoning on the identifiable victim effect') as if these are real empirical results. While the abstract does mention the dummy dataset, the framing presents these as actual study findings. Readers who only read the abstract would be misled into thinking real data were collected and analyzed.
issues.quote: We generated a dummy set of samples in the Qualtrics survey (N = 1000) and found no empirical support for the effect of analytical reasoning on the identifiable victim effect. To extend the replication, we added the 'perceived impact of donation' as a factor that is believed to be linked with the identifiable victim effect. Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics.

issues.subcategory: between-subjects design converted to within-subjects without justification
issues.description: The original Small et al. (2007) studies used between-subjects designs where participants were randomly assigned to conditions. The replication merges Studies 1 and 3 into a single experiment described as a 'within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables.' However, the procedures section states 'Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions,' which is neither a proper within-subjects nor between-subjects design but rather self-selection into conditions. This fundamentally undermines causal inference and introduces severe selection bias. Participants choosing their own condition cannot be used to draw conclusions about the causal effects of identifiability or intervention.
issues.quote: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables... Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

issues.subcategory: self-selection into experimental conditions
issues.description: Allowing participants to select their own experimental condition (identifiability and intervention) completely invalidates the experimental logic. Random assignment is the cornerstone of causal inference in experimental designs. If participants choose which condition to be in, any observed differences between conditions could be entirely due to pre-existing differences between the types of people who select each condition, not the manipulations themselves. This is a fatal flaw for a study attempting to replicate causal claims about deliberative thinking reducing donations.
issues.quote: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

issues.subcategory: imaginary donation replacing real donation
issues.description: The original study used real monetary donations (participants donated from $5 they had actually received). The replication uses imaginary donations ('Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter'). Research consistently shows that hypothetical and real donation decisions differ substantially. The identifiable victim effect and the impact of deliberative thinking may operate differently when no real money is at stake. This is a major deviation that could explain null results and limits comparability to the original.
issues.quote: Imaginary donation: Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.subcategory: merging two separate studies without adequate justification
issues.description: The replication merges Studies 1 and 3 from the original article into a single experiment. Study 1 tested explicit debiasing and Study 3 tested implicit debiasing through joint presentation. Combining these introduces demand characteristics, order effects, and potential contamination between conditions. The authors acknowledge this deviation but do not adequately address how merging the studies might affect the validity of each manipulation or the comparability of results to the original studies.
issues.quote: In this replication, we merged Studies 1 and 3 into one single experiment to study both the explicit and implicit intervention of debiasing the identifiable victim effect... The intervention of learning about the effect would also be applied to the joint condition to reveal a more comprehensive comparison between the explicit and implicit settings.

issues.subcategory: contradictory description of study design
issues.description: The Design section describes the study as a 'within-subject design,' but the original studies and the replication procedures describe between-subjects manipulations where participants are assigned to or select different conditions. A within-subjects design would require each participant to experience all conditions (identifiable victim, statistical victim, joint condition, intervention, no intervention), which would create obvious demand characteristics and carryover effects. The tables of descriptive statistics show different sample sizes per cell (e.g., 159, 175, 166), consistent with a between-subjects design, contradicting the within-subjects label.
issues.quote: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables

issues.subcategory: sample demographics implausible for MTurk study
issues.description: The simulated participant data reports a mean age of 67.80 (SD=30.10) with an age range of 18-120. A mean age of 67.8 is highly implausible for an Amazon Mechanical Turk sample, which typically skews younger (mean ages typically 30-40). An age range extending to 120 is biologically impossible. An SD of 30.10 with a mean of 67.80 would imply many participants below age 18 or above age 100. While these are acknowledged as simulated data, using such implausible values undermines the credibility of the simulation exercise and suggests inadequate quality control.
issues.quote: A total of 1000 responses were generated from the Qualtrics for pre-registration (Mage = 67.80, SD=30.10; 471 females and 529 males)... Average age (years): 67.8, Age range (years): 18-120

issues.subcategory: contradictory direction of identifiable victim effect in results
issues.description: The core hypothesis (Hypothesis 1) states 'People donate more to an identifiable victim than statistical victims,' consistent with the identifiable victim effect. However, the results report the opposite: 'participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).' The discussion does not adequately address this reversal of the expected effect direction, which would be a theoretically important finding if based on real data.
issues.quote: participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67)

issues.subcategory: post-hoc result contradicts hypothesis about perceived impact
issues.description: Hypothesis 6 states 'An identifiable victim elicits higher perceived impact of donation than statistical victims.' However, the post-hoc results show the significant difference is between the statistical victim condition and the joint condition (statistical vs. joint, p=.041), not between identifiable and statistical victims as hypothesized. The abstract claims 'people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics,' which is the opposite direction from Hypothesis 6. The abstract, hypothesis, and results are mutually inconsistent.
issues.quote: Significant differences were found between the statistical victim condition and the joint condition, t(994)=2.47, SE=0.11, p=.041. This suggested that participants who faced a statistical victim (M=3.12, SD=1.43) had a higher rating of perceived impact of their donation to help the victims than they faced an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics (M=2.85, SD=1.34).

issues.subcategory: ηp2 values inconsistent with reported F statistics and sample size
issues.description: In Table 9, the replication reports an F(2, 994) = 3.58, p = .028 for identifiability on donation, with ηp2 = .007. However, ηp2 = SSeffect / (SSeffect + SSerror). With F = 3.58, df1 = 2, df2 = 994, the expected ηp2 would be approximately (3.58 × 2) / (3.58 × 2 + 994) = 7.16/1001.16 ≈ .0072, which rounds to .007 and is consistent. However, the interaction F(2, 994) = 4.25, p = .015 yields ηp2 = (4.25 × 2)/(4.25 × 2 + 994) = 8.5/1002.5 ≈ .0085, which should round to .009, not .008 as reported. These are minor but indicate potential rounding or calculation errors.
issues.quote: Interaction... Replication | 2 | 4.25 | .015* | .008 | [0.00, 0.02]

issues.subcategory: confidence intervals for effect sizes include zero yet interpreted as significant
issues.description: Multiple effect size confidence intervals reported in Table 9 span [0.00, 0.02], meaning the lower bound is zero or effectively zero. For the identifiability effect (ηp2 = .007, 95%CI [0.00, 0.02]) and interaction effect (ηp2 = .008, 95%CI [0.00, 0.02]), the confidence intervals include zero, suggesting the true effect could be null. Yet these are reported as statistically significant (p = .028 and p = .015). This inconsistency between the p-value significance and CI including zero should be addressed, as it reflects the distinction between statistical significance and practical significance.
issues.quote: Identifiability... Replication | 2 | 3.58 | .028* | .007 | [0.00, 0.02]... Interaction... Replication | 2 | 4.25 | .015* | .008 | [0.00, 0.02]

issues.subcategory: post-hoc test confidence interval direction inconsistent with t-statistic sign
issues.description: In Table 10, the comparison 'Identifiable VS Statistical' reports t(994) = -2.40 with d = 0.076 and 95%CI [-0.05, 0.20]. A negative t-statistic indicates the identifiable condition mean is lower than the statistical condition mean, yet the effect size d is reported as positive (0.076) and the CI is predominantly positive [-0.05, 0.20]. The sign of d should be consistent with the direction of the t-statistic. Similarly in Table 14, 'Statistical VS Joint' reports t = 2.47, d = 0.08, 95%CI [-0.07, 0.23] — the CI crosses zero yet the comparison is reported as significant at p = .041 after Bonferroni correction, which is internally inconsistent.

issues.subcategory: Bonferroni-corrected p-value significant despite CI crossing zero
issues.description: In Table 14, the Statistical VS Joint comparison yields pBonferroni = .041 (significant) but the 95% CI for d is [-0.07, 0.23], which crosses zero. A significant p-value after Bonferroni correction should not correspond to a 95% CI that includes zero, as both are based on the same alpha level. This is a mathematical inconsistency that suggests either the CI or the p-value is incorrectly calculated.

issues.subcategory: original study effect sizes calculated post-hoc with undisclosed methods
issues.description: The authors state 'The effect size of the identifiable victim effect was not reported in the original study. Further calculation of the effect size and confidence interval was included in the supplementary.' The effect sizes reported (d = 0.48, d = -0.36, d = 0.41 for Study 1; d = 0.23 for Study 3) are used for power analysis and replication evaluation, but the methods for calculating these from the original reported statistics are not described in the main text. Without transparency about how these were derived, readers cannot verify their accuracy, and errors in these calculations would propagate to the power analysis and replication evaluation.
issues.quote: The effect size of the identifiable victim effect was not reported in the original study. Further calculation of the effect size and confidence interval was included in the supplementary under the section of 'Power analysis of the original study effect'. In Study 1, the main effect of identifiability on donation was d = 0.48, 95% CI [0.11, 0.84], while that of the intervention effect was d = -0.36, 95% CI [-0.72, 0.00].

issues.subcategory: no attention check or manipulation check described
issues.description: While the manuscript mentions excluding participants who 'failed the attention check,' no details are provided about what the attention check consists of, how many items it includes, or what the failure criterion is. More critically, there is no mention of manipulation checks to verify that the identifiability manipulation (identifiable vs. statistical victim) and the intervention manipulation (learning about the effect vs. not) were successfully implemented. Without manipulation checks, it is impossible to know whether null results reflect a true absence of the effect or a failed manipulation.
issues.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.

issues.subcategory: no blinding procedures described
issues.description: The manuscript does not describe any blinding procedures for data collection or analysis. Given that this is an online study on MTurk, participants could potentially identify the purpose of the study, especially in the intervention condition where they are explicitly taught about the identifiable victim effect. No mention is made of whether analysts were blinded to condition during data processing or whether any steps were taken to prevent demand characteristics.
issues.quote: Participants will conduct an online survey in Qualtrics on the Mechanical Amazon Turk platform while the original study surveyed inside a student center of a university in Pennsylvania

issues.subcategory: inappropriate causal language for correlational extension measure
issues.description: The extension hypothesis (Hypothesis 6) and its discussion treat perceived impact of donation as causally related to donation behavior and the identifiable victim effect. However, perceived impact is measured as a feeling variable alongside donation, not manipulated. The correlation analysis between feelings and donation cannot establish causal direction. The manuscript states 'with people having a stronger belief in the impact of their donation, they would be more willing to donate' as if this is an established causal relationship, but the design cannot test this.
issues.quote: Therefore, with people having a stronger belief in the impact of their donation, they would be more willing to donate.

issues.subcategory: confound introduced by applying intervention to joint condition
issues.description: The original Study 3 did not include an intervention condition for the joint condition. The replication adds intervention to the joint condition 'to allow the comparison of explicit and implicit manipulation with fewer confounds.' However, this actually introduces a new confound: participants in the joint/intervention condition receive both the explicit debiasing information AND the implicit debiasing through joint presentation. These two manipulations are now confounded in that cell, making it impossible to separate their effects. The claim that this reduces confounds is incorrect.
issues.quote: The intervention of learning about the effect would also be applied to the joint condition to reveal a more comprehensive comparison between the explicit and implicit settings.

issues.subcategory: MTurk sample generalizability not adequately discussed
issues.description: The original study used a convenience sample from a university student center in Pennsylvania. The replication uses MTurk workers, who differ systematically from both student samples and the general population in terms of attention, motivation, experience with online surveys, and demographic characteristics. The manuscript acknowledges this as a contextual variable difference but does not discuss how this might affect the replicability of the findings or limit generalizability of the results.
issues.quote: MTurk workers as participants: We will recruit participants on the Mechanical Amazon Turk platform while the original study recruited participants sitting inside the school centre of a university in Pennsylvania

issues.subcategory: updated victim information changes stimulus validity
issues.description: The replication uses updated victim information from Save the Children's website rather than the original stimuli. The identifiable victim effect is known to be sensitive to the specific characteristics of the victim presented (name, age, face, story). Using different victim information means the stimuli are not equivalent to the original study, and any differences in results could be attributable to differences in the stimuli rather than the underlying psychological mechanisms. This is classified as a 'similar' deviation but its potential impact on results is not adequately discussed.
issues.quote: Updated victim information: We will present the participants with the most updated victim information retrieved from the website of Save the Children given that those used in the original study was dated two decades ago.

issues.subcategory: pre-registration status unclear given simulated data
issues.description: The manuscript claims to be pre-registered and provides an OSF link, but the results are based on simulated random data. It is unclear whether the pre-registration was filed before or after the simulated analyses were run, and whether the analysis plan was developed based on the simulated results. If the analysis plan was refined based on what the simulated data showed, this would constitute a form of analytic flexibility that undermines the value of pre-registration. The authorship declaration states 'Gilad supervised each step in the project, conducted the pre-registrations, and ran data collection,' suggesting data collection may have already occurred, yet results are still presented as simulated.
issues.quote: Pre-registration on the Open Science Framework: https://osf.io/n4jkh/?view_only=d52771c7540a4a8f8051c8b430a6f15d... Data collection for the experiment was launched at the start of the study period.

issues.subcategory: conditional analysis decisions not fully pre-specified
issues.description: Several analyses are described as conditional on prior results (e.g., 'Note: we conduct the test only if the interaction effect is significant' for post-hoc contrast tests, and 'Note: We conduct the test only if the effect of identifiability and intervention are significant' for Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise comparisons). While these conditions are stated, the thresholds and exact decision rules are not fully specified, leaving room for researcher discretion in determining when to conduct follow-up analyses.
issues.quote: Post-hoc contrast test (Note: we conduct the test only if the interaction effect is significant)... Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise comparisons (Note: We conduct the test only if the effect of identifiability and intervention are significant)

issues.subcategory: exclusion criteria applied to simulated data without real attrition information
issues.description: The manuscript describes excluding participants with prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect and those failing attention checks, but since the data are simulated, no actual exclusions occurred. The manuscript does not specify what proportion of participants would be expected to be excluded, what the minimum sample size after exclusions would need to be to maintain adequate power, or how missing data would be handled. The power analysis presumably was conducted on the full N=1000, but post-exclusion sample sizes could be substantially smaller.
issues.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.

issues.subcategory: aggregated feelings scale validity not established
issues.description: The manuscript describes combining multiple distinct affective reactions (being upset, being touched, being sympathetic, moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, and perceived impact) into a single 'aggregated feeling' score. No justification is provided for why these conceptually distinct constructs should be combined, no reliability analysis (e.g., Cronbach's alpha) is reported or planned, and no factor analysis is mentioned to verify that these items form a coherent scale. Perceived impact of donation is conceptually different from emotional reactions and its inclusion in an aggregated feelings score is particularly questionable.
issues.quote: Note: combine segregated feelings into one aggregated feeling... Note: Segregated feelings include being upsetting, being touched, being sympathetic, moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, and perceived impact of donation (extension)

issues.subcategory: perceived impact operationalization not described
issues.description: The extension measure 'perceived impact of donation' is introduced as a key construct but its operationalization is never described in the main text. No information is provided about how many items measure it, what the scale anchors are, whether it is a single item or multi-item scale, or how it was validated. This makes it impossible to evaluate whether the measure has construct validity or to replicate the measurement.
issues.quote: We aim to extend the replication study by considering the 'perceived impact of donation' as one of the feeling variables indicated in Small et al. (2007)'s Study 1.

issues.subcategory: misattribution of availability heuristic to identifiable victim effect
issues.description: The manuscript attributes the identifiable victim effect partly to the 'availability heuristic' (ease of retrieving instances from memory). However, the identifiable victim effect is more accurately explained by the affect heuristic and the vividness/concreteness of identified individuals, not by memory retrieval ease. The availability heuristic concerns frequency judgments based on ease of recall, which is a different mechanism. The original Small et al. (2007) paper itself emphasizes the affect heuristic, not availability. This theoretical mischaracterization could lead to incorrect predictions and interpretations.
issues.quote: The 'availability heuristic' (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973), which relies on the ease of retrieving relevant instances from memory, is believed to be activated when we value a personalized individual (Small & Loewenstein, 2003). The information we receive about this person may elicit stronger affective reactions such as sympathy and distress

issues.subcategory: proportion dominance explanation misapplied
issues.description: The manuscript's explanation of proportion dominance states that 'a higher proportion of lives usually generate more helpfulness.' However, the proportion dominance effect in the identifiable victim literature refers to the proportion of a reference group that can be saved, not the absolute proportion of lives. The explanation that an identifiable victim has a 100% rescue proportion because 'the victim himself serving as the reference only' is a post-hoc rationalization that conflates the reference group with the victim, which is not how proportion dominance is typically operationalized or tested.
issues.quote: For the case of an identifiable victim, given that the reference group is salient with the victim himself serving as the reference only, the proportion is as high as 100%.

issues.subcategory: power analysis not reported in main text
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly refers readers to the supplementary for power analysis details ('The full report of power analysis can be found in the supplementary'). Power analysis is a critical methodological detail that should be reported in the main text, including the target effect size, alpha level, desired power, and resulting required sample size. Without this information in the main text, readers cannot evaluate whether the study is adequately powered.
issues.quote: The sample size for this study was determined to ensure adequate statistical power for detecting the effects reported in the original study. The full report of power analysis can be found in the supplementary under the section of 'Power analysis of the original study effect'.

issues.subcategory: stimulus materials not provided in main text
issues.description: The actual text of the charity request letters, the intervention materials (text about the identifiable victim effect), and the victim descriptions are not provided in the main text. These are critical for evaluating the validity of the manipulations and for replication. The manuscript only provides a link to a Qualtrics survey, which may not be permanently accessible.
issues.quote: For the full reported survey, please access the Qualtrics survey with the link below: https://www.dropbox.com/sh/9sda2czfg6rzko3/AACsg1vIzXhMOInM7XMtV5ILa?dl=0

issues.subcategory: incomplete links and placeholder text in manuscript
issues.description: The manuscript contains multiple placeholder entries indicating it is incomplete: 'Cloud folder for presentation (PPT and PDF): <enter link here>' and 'Cloud folder for peer reviews: <enter link here>'. These suggest the manuscript was submitted before completion. Additionally, several in-text links appear to be broken or formatted incorrectly (e.g., 'supplementary' appearing as inline text that seems to be a hyperlink label without proper formatting).
issues.quote:
Cloud folder for presentation (PPT and PDF) | <enter link here>
Cloud folder for peer reviews | <enter link here>

issues.subcategory: feeling variables measurement scale not described
issues.description: The manuscript does not describe the response scales used for the feeling variables (being upset, being touched, being sympathetic, moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, perceived impact). The number of scale points, anchors, and whether items were adapted from validated scales are not reported. This information is essential for evaluating construct validity and for replication.
issues.quote: These items included beliefs about the severity of the crisis, the perceived trustworthiness of the charity, the expected accountability of funds, evaluation of organizational efficiency, and the appropriateness of donation to help the victims.

issues.subcategory: Table 1 presents same F-statistic for all rows
issues.description: In Table 1, the F-statistic of 6.75 and p < .05 are listed for both the overall identifiability effect AND for each individual condition (identifiable victim and statistical victim separately). Similarly, F = 4.15 is listed for both the intervention effect and for each intervention condition. F-statistics from an ANOVA apply to the overall effect, not to individual condition means. Reporting the same F-statistic for individual group means is statistically meaningless and suggests a misunderstanding of ANOVA output.

issues.subcategory: residual df inconsistency between original study tables
issues.description: Table 1 reports residual df = 115 for Study 1 (N=121), which is consistent with a 2×2 design (121 - 4 - 1 = 116, or 121 - 6 = 115). Table 12 (replication) reports residual df = 114 for the original study aggregated feelings analysis, while Table 9 reports residual df = 115 for the original study donation analysis. If both analyses used the same sample (N=121) with the same design, the residual df should be identical. This discrepancy is unexplained.
issues.quote: Residual... Original study | 114... [in Table 12] vs. Original study | 115 [in Table 9]

issues.subcategory: no control for multiple comparisons across hypotheses
issues.description: The study tests six hypotheses (H1-H6) with multiple statistical tests for each, including separate ANOVAs for donation, aggregated feelings, and six segregated feeling variables. No correction for multiple comparisons across the family of tests is applied or discussed. With 18+ statistical tests conducted, the probability of at least one false positive is substantially elevated. The only correction mentioned is Bonferroni adjustment within post-hoc pairwise comparisons, not across the broader set of hypothesis tests.
issues.quote: We conducted a 2 (intervention) X 3 (identifiability) two way ANOVA to examine the effect of identifiability and intervention on segregated affective reactions which were combined to form an aggregated feeling in the previous statistical tests.

issues.subcategory: unequal cell sizes not addressed
issues.description: The descriptive statistics tables show unequal cell sizes across conditions (e.g., identifiable/intervention n=159, statistical/intervention n=175, joint/intervention n=166, identifiable/no intervention n=175, statistical/no intervention n=159, joint/no intervention n=166). The manuscript does not explain why cell sizes are unequal (presumably due to self-selection into conditions), does not report whether Type I, II, or III sums of squares were used in the ANOVA, and does not address whether unequal cell sizes affect the validity of the ANOVA results.
